title: Bearing the arrow (320–324)
hookLine: as the elephant in battle bears the arrow, I will bear harsh words
last: THE FRONTIER FORT — GUARD THE BORDER TOWN.

cards: Someone says something harsh about you. Online, across a table, or behind your back, and it comes around. Your body reacts before you do: face hot, heart fast, a reply already typing itself in your head.
And a small voice says: let's just leave. Change the group chat, the job, the town. The old commentary on today's verse tells of a morning when the Buddha's companion said almost exactly that.

teach.b: Verse three hundred twenty, in Max Müller's English: "Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured."
The commentary's story: in the city of Kosambi, a woman named Magandiya held a grudge against the Buddha. She paid people to follow him and his monks through the streets, shouting insults.
Ananda, a monk traveling with the Buddha, had had enough.
Let's go to another town, he said. The Buddha asked: and if they abuse us there? Then another town, said Ananda.
The Buddha said a problem should be settled where it arises, and he spoke this verse. The abuse, the story says, faded within a week.
The picture is a war elephant, trained to walk into battle and take the arrows that come at it.
A tamed elephant, the next verses say, is the one the king rides, and the best among people is the one who has tamed himself and can bear hard words.

Mules, fine horses and great elephants are good when trained, but the one who trains himself is better still. No animal, however fine, can carry you to the untrodden place; only a tamed self goes there.
Bearing isn't pretending it didn't hurt.

The arrow still lands. The elephant just doesn't stampede. Buddhist teaching calls this khanti, patience or forbearance, one of the qualities a person on the path trains, again and again, one arrow at a time.

how: Buddhist teachers pair verse 320 with the commentary's story of Magandiya's hired insults; khanti, patience, is trained as a daily practice and counted among the perfections in both Theravada and Mahayana teaching.

o: an elephant: a picture of calmly bearing harsh words
a royal guard who silences anyone who insults
a war horse trained to charge at the first arrow

games.q: match each person or picture in today's story.

s: bearing the arrow means pretending it didn't hurt
the arrow still lands; the elephant just doesn't stampede.
in the story, the Buddha agreed to move to another town
he said a problem should be settled where it arises.
the verses say the one who tames himself is best of all
better than trained mules, horses or elephants.

games.q: you're Ananda. strangers are shouting insults at your teacher every day in Kosambi. what do you suggest?
games.why: Ananda suggested leaving. the Buddha asked what they'd do if the next town did the same, stayed, and spoke verse 320. the story says the insults faded within a week.

practice: Feet on the ground, heavy like an elephant, bring back one small criticism you've received lately, and notice where the words land in the body: the chest, the jaw, the belly.
Don't argue with them, and don't agree either; just stand, feeling the sting without turning to trample, and breathe into that spot. Then let the criticism go, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Nāga. An elephant: like a war elephant that takes the arrow and doesn't stampede, this is patience with harsh words.

orig.note: Pali nāga: an elephant (also a serpent, or a great being); the chapter's name is Nāgavagga.

carryVoice: Your line: bear the arrow. Like the elephant, stand your ground. That's day two hundred sixteen.
